author: opt-B4

contract.sync_assumed: caller separates consecutive calls that reuse the temp storage by a block barrier
contract.sync_performed: __syncthreads inside: as B1_n6b (1 init, 2 per pass), plus 1 before the warp finish when the pivot bin after the first pass holds at most 32 items
contract.n_range: N = Threads x IPT, Threads 128, 256 or 512, N <= 32768, prefer_smaller_index up to IPT 64 (N6's tie mask), measured N 1024 and 4096 at 256 threads
contract.type_constraints: fp32 and bf16 keys, int32 indices derived from the striped position
contract.nan_behavior: as B1_n6b: NaN unsupported, -0.0 folded onto +0.0 under prefer_smaller_index only; the warp finish treats the all-ones packed word as the empty-slot sentinel (a negative NaN with a full mantissa, never produced by focus-set inputs)
contract.tie_break_support: both requirements: the warp finish orders the pivot bin by (key descending, index ascending), so it is exact under prefer_smaller_index without N6's warp-redundant rank; the items above the pivot bin are scattered by ticket as in N6
contract.sorted_output_support: not supported inherently, post-sort of k

correctness_notes: All 48 cells passed the oracle battery (13 cases per cell) under both requirements, including signed_zero under prefer_smaller_index (N6's normalization) and tie_heavy and pivot_tie (the pivot bin exceeds 32 there and the N6 passes run unchanged).

low_level: The pivot bin's members draw a ticket with atomicAdd with return on one constant shared address and store a (twiddled key, inverted index) pair to a 32-word buffer, warp 0 loads one pair per lane after a barrier and runs k_rem rounds: one redux.max per round on the packed word (key16 << 16 | inverted index) for bf16, two for fp32 (the key, then the inverted index among the lanes holding that key). The items above the pivot bin keep N6's per-item ticket scatter.

Registers of the latency kernel: 46 at N 1024 and 80 at N 4096 under not_guaranteed (identical to B1_n6b), 58 and 128 under prefer_smaller_index against 58 and 128 for B1_n6b, so the finish adds no registers and no spill. Temp storage grows by 264 bytes (the pivot buffer and its counter).

The constant-address pivot ticket is of the kind ptxas warp-aggregates (T23: S2R SR_LANEID and SR_LTMASK, VOTE, POPC, elected atomic, SHFL per site), one site per item slot; the second build N9_w2fin2 draws both tickets from one class-indexed counter as B1_idx does and is measured separately.
algorithmic: Against B1_n6b in the same lock section (B200, cycles per call, random normal input): under not_guaranteed the warp finish is slower in every cell, bf16 N 1024 k 16 1770 against 1688 (plus 5 percent), k 64 2095 against 2042, k 256 2359 against 2333, N 4096 k 16 2957 against 2749 (plus 8 percent), k 64 4107 against 4043, k 256 5082 against 4570 (plus 11 percent), fp32 N 1024 k 16 1800 against 1664 (plus 8 percent), N 4096 k 256 5010 against 4464 (plus 12 percent). Under prefer_smaller_index it is faster in every cell: bf16 N 1024 k 16 1989 against 2233 (minus 11 percent), N 4096 k 64 4403 against 6193 (minus 29 percent), k 256 5414 against 6913 (minus 22 percent), fp32 N 1024 k 16 2022 against 2094 (minus 3 percent), N 4096 k 64 4408 against 5096 (minus 14 percent), k 256 5361 against 5979 (minus 10 percent). Throughput follows the same signs (bf16 N 4096 k 64 prefer_smaller_index 413 against 298 Gelem per s).

Why the not_guaranteed cells lose: N6b already ends after the first pass by count or by the tie class in most rows of the kill cell (the host simulation puts the first-pass exit at 0.97 of the bf16 N 1024 k 16 rows and 0.73 of the fp32 rows), so the second pass that N9 removes is rarely executed there, while the warp-finish path adds a ticket per item slot, a barrier, the buffer round trip and the rounds to every row it takes. Where the second pass does run often (fp32 N 4096 k 256, first-pass exit 0.14) the finish still costs more than the pass it replaces, which points at the aggregated constant-address tickets (one dependent S2R chain per item slot, 16 slots at N 4096) rather than at the rounds (k_rem is 1 to 7).

Why the prefer_smaller_index cells win: the warp finish is exact on (key, index) by construction and replaces N6's warp-redundant rank (ballot table, barrier, shuffle scan over the slots) for the ties, which is the whole gap of 10 to 29 percent between N6b's two requirements at these cells.
negative: The N9 kill criterion fails: N9 does not take 15 percent off B1_n6b at N 1024 k 16 bf16 (1770 against 1688, threshold 1430) nor at N 4096 (2957 against 2749, threshold 2340) under not_guaranteed. The card's cost model charged N6 a full second pass per call and credited the finish with about 150 fixed cycles, both wrong by the measurement: the pass runs in a minority of rows and the finish costs more than 150 cycles with constant-address tickets.
The two-redux fp32 round (key, then inverted index) is as fast as the one-redux bf16 round within the noise at these k_rem (1 to 7 rounds), so the round form is not what separates the two types here.
surprises: The same code is a 10 to 29 percent gain under prefer_smaller_index: at block scope the cheapest exact tie resolution for a small pivot set is a warp of redux rounds on (key, index), not a block-wide rank, which also holds for B4's finish.
N6b's first-pass exit rate on bf16 logits is so high (the pivot bin is a single bf16 value in nearly every row from N 4096 on) that the second pass is already a rare path for bf16 at k at most 64.
open_questions: N9_w2fin2 (one class-indexed ticket per item as in B1_idx) isolates the aggregation cost of the constant-address ticket, batch n9b.

A finish that skips the ticket entirely (the pivot members are at most 32, a ballot per item slot and a warp-level prefix would place them without atomics) was not built; T22 says per-slot ballots form a dependent chain, so the gain is unclear.
Whether N6b itself should take the W2 finish only under prefer_smaller_index (where it replaces the rank) and keep the second pass under not_guaranteed.
